headline: US spending on building data centres grew 64.5% in the latest year while nearly every other kind of construction shrank, according to figures used in an essay by the writer Derek Thompson.
score_reason: Pool 4 kept: the full Futurism text was read, but the figures come second-hand from an essay and an economist's data that were not read, and Futurism's reading is opinion.
importance_line: What changed is a sharper picture of how lopsided US building has become, which matters first to builders, workers and towns where housing, hospital and factory construction is falling, then to anyone relying on the economy's growth, and the doubt is that these are an essay's figures relayed by Futurism, whose view that the growth is unhealthy is opinion.
summary: Futurism reports on an essay by the writer and podcaster Derek Thompson, which uses data from Harvard Kennedy School economist Jason Furman to show US spending on data-centre construction up 64.5% over the most recent year and new energy infrastructure up 4.1%, while multi-family housing fell 5.6%, healthcare and commercial retail building 10.1%, educational building 12.6% and manufacturing nearly 24% from 2025 to 2026. Futurism adds its own view that this growth is 'predicated almost entirely on the AI boom' and could fall back if investors lose faith in AI spending, which is the outlet's judgment, not a finding of the data.
notes: Futurism's text read in full (fulltext). The essay by Derek Thompson and Furman's data were not read; the essay's date and place are not stated. Futurism published on 11 Oct 2026.
